SATOM 1.7.0

Introduces the AI Advisor for false-positive triage and Lua drafting, and adds sealed recovery custody so a rebuilt node can read its restored secrets.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user
On this page
  • In short
  • What's new
  • AI Advisor
  • Recovery custody for the secrets no backup carries
  • What changes for you
  • Fixed
  • Before you upgrade
  • Under the hood
  • Learn more

Released: 2026-08-07 · All releases

In short#

1.7.0 introduces the AI Advisor, a read-only assistant for WAF false-positive triage, Lua script drafting and configuration search. For administrators it adds recovery custody: a protected way to keep the two secrets no backup carries, so an installation can be rebuilt from a backup. It also fixes a series of health checks that reported "fine" when they could not actually tell.

What's new#

AI Advisor#

A chat assistant (Settings → AI Advisor) that helps you triage WAF false positives, draft Lua scripts and search the device configuration source of truth.

  • Local by default. It uses a local AI model, so no data leaves your network. External providers (OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic) are opt-in behind an explicit "allow external providers" setting.
  • You see what leaves the network. When an external provider is used, known internal names are removed first and you get a preview of exactly what will be sent.
  • It never writes anything. A proposed WAF exception or Lua script becomes a pending proposal, which turns into a draft in the normal exception or Lua lists, behind the same permissions the manual forms require.
  • Device data such as WAF logs and policy content is clearly marked as untrusted in what is sent to the model, to resist prompt injection.
  • Two new permissions control it: one to use the Advisor and one to configure it.

Recovery custody for the secrets no backup carries#

SATOM has two secrets that are deliberately left out of backups, standby synchronisation and version control: the key that opens every encrypted value in the database, and the internal certificate authority key. Without them, a backup restored onto a rebuilt node holds secrets nobody can read.

  • Sealed envelope. The two secrets can now be sealed into an envelope protected by a passphrase. The envelope is copied to the standby within five minutes and is included in every backup from then on. Someone who steals a backup only gets encrypted data; you, holding the passphrase, can rebuild the installation from any copy.
  • The passphrase is created at installation, so a standalone node is covered too. A standby receives it when it joins the pair, so both nodes open the same envelope.
  • Key check on restore. Backups now record a fingerprint of the key (which identifies it without revealing it). A restore compares it and tells you by name if the key does not match.
  • Audited export and a recovery check. You can export the recovery key through an audited command, and a recovery check reports when the secrets have never been exported, or when the envelope is missing, unreadable or out of date.

What changes for you#

  • Site-specific redaction rules are now copied to the standby and included in backups. Before, this file was carried by nothing, so a standby could run for days with outdated rules. The old location is still read so existing nodes keep working.
  • A missing or broken redaction rules file is now reported as an error on a deployed installation, instead of quietly redacting less.
  • Backups now include node-local configuration. On restore it is only placed where the node has none, because the live copy is more likely to be current.
  • Documentation corrected. A retired mechanism was still described as live in the install manual and on the High Availability page; that is removed. The System Backup page no longer makes claims about your infrastructure and tells you what to check instead. The restore guide no longer claims a total loss can be recovered from a backup alone.

Fixed#

  • Nine health checks answered "I could not tell" with "fine". Among them: scoping fell back to the Global console and showed every product; a damaged access-control entry read as "no restriction"; an unreadable repository reported itself clean; high availability was taken as standalone and the standby check skipped; a safety check before a reset reported "nothing to keep"; hypervisor certificate checks reported "verified" without using your certificate authority; an unreadable SSH host-key store was treated as a first connection; an unreadable colour skipped the contrast check. Each now reports a separate "could not tell" state.
  • Hypervisor certificate checking never used your imported certificate authority, only public ones. It does now.
  • Two SSH connections accepted any host key: the automatic certificate pull and the ESXi shell connection. Both now pin host keys like the rest of SATOM; a genuinely new host is still trusted on first contact.
  • Updates did not refresh some service definitions, and some installed services still referred to an account that no longer exists.
  • Helper scripts outside the application had no installer, and the replication helper was months out of date, so it could report success while replicating nothing.

Before you upgrade#

  • After upgrading, plan to export the recovery key and keep the seal passphrase outside the fleet. Note that sealing in this version has a defect fixed in 1.7.1; if you sealed on 1.7.0, seal again after upgrading to 1.7.1.

Under the hood#

  • One shared implementation of SSH host-key pinning is now used for every SSH connection SATOM opens.
  • A new check stops private-key text from being written into the source code, so it is caught when the change is made rather than by aborting a release.
